source_batch.unit_label: BRBL Module A unit 1: legal framework of regulation of banks

facts.statement: Banking and the sources of regulation (courseware): banking in India is mainly governed by the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934; the Reserve Bank and the Government exercise control over banks from the opening to winding up by virtue of powers under these Acts. The regulatory provisions are not uniformly applicable to all banks: applicability depends on the constitution of the bank, that is, whether it is a statutory corporation, a banking company or a co-operative society. The definition of banking in Section 5(b) of the Banking Regulation Act: accepting, for the purpose of lending or investing, deposits of money from the public, repayable on demand or otherwise and withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise. A bank therefore performs two essential functions: acceptance of deposits from the public and lending or investment of such deposits. Deposits may be repayable on demand or after a period as agreed; accepting deposits from the public does not mean the banker accepts from anyone who offers money (a banker can refuse to open accounts of undesirable persons and opening is subject to know-your-customer norms, which also require monitoring suspicious transactions for reporting under anti-money laundering and countering terrorism financing measures).

Deposits, non-banking entities and the licence (courseware): under Section 49A no person other than a banking company, the Reserve Bank, the State Bank of India or any other banking institution, firm or other person notified by the Central Government is authorised to accept for the payment of money any deposit withdrawable by cheque. Non-banking financial companies and some other firms and associations accept deposits from the public; acceptance by non-banking financial companies is regulated by the Reserve Bank under the Non-Banking Financial Companies Acceptance of Public Deposits (Reserve Bank) Directions, 1998 and other directions under Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act. A licence from the Reserve Bank under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act is necessary to commence or carry on the business of banking in India. Every banking company has to use the word bank as part of its name (Section 7) and no company other than a banking company can use the words bank, banker or banking as a part of its name; no firm, individual or group of individuals may use the words bank, banking or banker as a part of the name or for the purpose of its business. Subsidiaries of banks and associations of banks in certain cases, primary credit societies and a co-operative society formed for the protection of mutual interest of co-operative banks and any co-operative society formed by the employees of a banking company, not being a primary credit society, and the State Bank of India or nationalised banks are exempted from this restriction.

Permitted and prohibited business (courseware): the main business of banks is acceptance of deposits and lending or investing, but banks carry on many allied business activities. Activities permitted under Section 6(1) include dealing in bills of exchange (drawing, accepting, buying, selling, collecting), lending or advancing money, carrying on and transacting every kind of guarantee and indemnity business, managing, selling and realising any property which may come into the possession of the bank in satisfaction or part satisfaction of any of its claims, and others; the Central Government may notify other business under Section 6(1). Prohibited business (Section 8): a banking company shall not engage directly or indirectly in trading activities and shall not undertake trading risks; buying, selling or bartering of goods is prohibited; goods mean every kind of moveable property other than actionable claims, stocks, shares, money, bullion and specie and instruments referred to in Section 6(1). This does not prejudice business permitted under Section 6(1); a bank can realise securities given to it or held by it for a loan, if need arises for the realisation of the amount lent. It can also buy or sell or barter for others in connection with bills of exchange received for collection or negotiation and undertake the administration of estates as executor or trustee. Section 9 (disposal of non-banking assets): no banking company shall hold any immovable property howsoever acquired, except as required for its own use, for any period exceeding seven years from the acquisition thereof; the property shall be disposed of within such period or extended period; the Reserve Bank may extend the period by up to five years where it is satisfied that the extension would be in the interests of the depositors.

Constitution of banks (courseware): banks in India fall under one of the categories: a body corporate constituted under a special statute; a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956 (Companies Act, 2013) or a foreign company; or a co-operative society registered under a Central or state enactment. Public sector banks (other than the State Bank of India) are constituted under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts of 1970 and 1980: under Section 3 of these Acts the Central Government nationalised (took over the business of) certain banking companies and vested them in newly created statutory bodies (corresponding new banks). The State Bank of India was constituted under the State Bank of India Act, 1955 and the seven associate or subsidiary banks under the State Bank (Subsidiary Banks) Act, 1959; the seven subsidiaries and associates were merged with the State Bank of India, completed in the financial year 2017-18. Regional Rural Banks were constituted under the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976 and are governed by the statutes creating them as well as some provisions of the Banking Regulation Act and the Reserve Bank of India Act. Most private sector banks (including micro and small finance banks) are companies constituted under the Companies Act; foreign banks are foreign companies constituted under statutes abroad and treated as such under Section 2(42) of the Companies Act, 2013; certain provisions of the Companies Act apply as provided, and all foreign companies transacting banking in India are governed by the Banking Regulation Act and the RBI Act regarding their banking business.

Co-operative banks (courseware): a co-operative bank conducts ordinary banking business but is established on a co-operative basis. Co-operative credit institutions are urban co-operative banks (scheduled and non-scheduled, multi-state or single state) and rural co-operatives: long term (state co-operative agriculture and rural development banks and primary co-operative agriculture and rural development banks) and short term (state co-operative banks, district central co-operative banks and primary agricultural credit societies). If a co-operative bank operates in more than one state, the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act applies; otherwise the respective state Co-operative Societies Act applies. By the Banking Laws (Application to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1965, certain provisions of the Banking Regulation Act and the RBI Act were extended to the co-operative banking sector (Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act with effect from 1965). Over the years problems in co-operative banks (the PMC Bank failure in Mumbai in 2019-20) led to the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020, in force from 29 September 2020 as stated in the courseware, giving the Reserve Bank more regulatory control over the management, capital, audit and liquidation of co-operative banks, including powers of supersession of the board and restructuring and the reconstruction of such banks. The amended Section 56 modifies references: banking company becomes co-operative bank, commencement of the Act becomes commencement of the Banking Laws (Application to Co-operative Societies) Act, memorandum or articles become bye-laws, and Registrar of Companies becomes the Central or State Registrar of Co-operative Societies. Co-operative banks may raise capital through public or private issues of equity, preference shares and debentures but this does not affect the existing powers of the State Registrars. For co-operative banks registered under the deposit insurance and credit guarantee law the Reserve Bank can order winding up in specified circumstances. Control is dual: State Governments and the Registrar under the Co-operative Societies Act control formation, management and winding up; the Reserve Bank controls banking licensing and regulation of banking business.

Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 (courseware): the Act was enacted to constitute the Reserve Bank, with the primary aim to regulate the issue of bank notes and to keep reserves to secure monetary stability and generally to operate the currency and credit system to the country advantage. It deals with the constitution, powers and functions of the Reserve Bank and does not directly deal with regulation of the banking system except for Section 42, which provides for cash reserves of scheduled banks to be kept with the Reserve Bank so as to regulate the credit system and ensure monetary stability; Section 18 provides for direct discount of bills of exchange and promissory notes. The general superintendence and direction of affairs is vested in the Central Board of Directors consisting of a Governor and not more than four deputy governors appointed by the Central Government; four directors nominated by the Central Government, one from each of the local boards; ten directors nominated by the Central Government; and two government officials nominated by the Government. A scheduled bank is one included in the Second Schedule of the RBI Act, which includes only those banks that satisfy the criteria in Section 42(6)(a). Other sections: constitution (Section 3), capital (Section 4), management (Section 7), composition of the Central Board and term of office (Section 8), business the bank may transact (Section 17 and not transact Section 19), issue of bank notes (Section 22), power of the Central Government to supersede the Central Board (Section 30), and cash reserve requirement of scheduled banks (Section 42). The Reserve Bank acts as lender of last resort (an institution offering funds to banks or other financial institutions that are experiencing financial difficulty or are considered highly risky) under Sections 17 and 18. Non-banking financial company amendments in 2019 (Chapter VI of the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2019) gave the Reserve Bank powers to replace or supersede the board of a regulated non-banking financial company, remove or debar auditors, frame schemes for amalgamation, reconstruction or splitting into viable and non-viable businesses, and direct group company statements and inspection.

Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (courseware): a comprehensive legislation regulating banks, passed as the Banking Companies Act 1949 and in force from 16 March 1949; renamed the Banking Regulation Act from 1 March 1966; applied to Jammu and Kashmir from 1956; extended to co-operative banks in 1965 by adding Section 56. The Act covers the definition of banking, licensing, capital and reserve requirements, banking operations and management structure, liquidity provisions, bank inspection and the takeover, amalgamation and liquidation of banks. The Reserve Bank has powers to license banks, regulate shareholding and voting rights, supervise the appointment of the board and managers, regulate the operations, lay down instructions for audits, issue moratorium, mergers and liquidation, issue directives in the interest of public good and on banking policy and impose penalties. Amendments: the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2017 inserted Sections 35AA and 35AB empowering the Reserve Bank to issue directions to any banking company to initiate insolvency resolution in default cases under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016; the 2012 amendment set up the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund to take over inoperative deposit accounts not claimed or operated for ten years; the Reserve Bank conducts an annual financial inspection of banking companies under Section 35 and risk-based supervision through the Supervisory Program on Assessment of Risk and Capital. Objectives of the Banking Regulation Act: provide specific legislation to the business of banking in India; prevent bank failures by prescribing minimum capital requirements; ensure balanced development and growth of banking companies; give specific powers to the Reserve Bank; and safeguard the interest of depositors.

Reserve Bank and Government as regulators (courseware): the Reserve Bank is the regulator of banks and other financial institutions such as non-banking financial companies; the Department of Non-Banking Supervision is entrusted with regulation and supervision of non-banking financial companies under Chapter III B and C and Chapter V of the RBI Act. Major powers of the Reserve Bank as regulator and supervisor: power to issue banking licences; power of appointment and removal of managerial personnel or boards; power to regulate the business of banks; power to give directions; power to inspect and supervise banks; power regarding audit of banks; power to collect, collate and furnish credit information; power relating to moratorium, amalgamation and winding up; and power to impose penalties. The Government of India is the sole shareholder of the Reserve Bank; the Governor and members of the Central Board are appointed by the Government who also have powers to remove them. Under Section 7(1) of the RBI Act the Government can give directions to the Reserve Bank in the public interest in consultation with the Governor; the courseware notes this power was supposed to be used rarely and was first used in October 2018 when letters were sent on liquidity for non-banking financial companies, capital requirement for weak banks and lending to small enterprises. Government powers to influence Reserve Bank decisions include appellate authority in several matters: appeal against removal of managerial personnel (Section 10B and 36AA of the Banking Regulation Act); appeals against cancellation of a banking licence (Section 22) and refusal of a certificate on floating charges (Section 14A); suspension of operations or exemption from provisions of the Act (Sections 4 and 53 respectively) on recommendation of the Reserve Bank; notification of other business banks may engage in (Section 6(1)); rule making (Sections 52 and 45Y on preservation of records); approval for formation of a subsidiary for certain business (Section 19); notification of accounts and balance sheet (Section 29); directions for inspection (Section 35); powers to acquire undertakings of banks (Section 36AE); and appointment of a court liquidator attached to the High Court under Section 38A. The Central Government has substantial control over the management of public sector banks (50 per cent or more of the shares of State Bank of India, nationalised banks and regional rural banks are held by the Central Government); only certain provisions of the Banking Regulation Act apply to these banks as indicated in that Act.

Regulation by other authorities (courseware): a banking company is subject to the control of other regulatory agencies in the conduct of its business: under the Companies Act in respect of company matters; to labour authorities in respect of service terms of workmen, opening and closing of premises and engagement of contract labour; to income tax and other taxes such as cash transaction tax and goods and services tax. As provided in Section 6 of the Banking Regulation Act, banks may undertake certain non-banking business in addition to the business of banking and are then subject to the control of other agencies: dealings in securities like shares and debentures are subject to regulation by the Securities and Exchange Board of India under the Securities Contract (Regulation) Act, 1956 read with the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992; if a bank wishes to raise capital through public issue it has to comply with SEBI guidelines; insurance business must follow Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority regulations, and mutual fund and merchant banking business follow Reserve Bank and SEBI rules.

payload.title: Sources of banking regulation and the definition of banking
payload.core_explanation_md:
Banking in India is governed mainly by the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**. The Reserve Bank and the Government control banks **from opening to winding up**.

**The provisions do not apply uniformly**: they depend on whether the bank is a **statutory corporation**, a **banking company** or a **co-operative society**.

**Definition (Section 5(b), as the courseware cites it):** *accepting, for the purpose of **lending or investing**, **deposits of money from the public**, **repayable on demand or otherwise** and **withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise**.*

So a bank does **two essential things:** **accepts deposits from the public** and **lends or invests** them. Accepting from the public does **not** mean accepting from anyone: a bank can **refuse undesirable customers**, and account opening follows **KYC norms**, with **suspicious transactions reported** under anti-money laundering rules.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A deposit-taker that does not lend or invest the deposits is not a bank under the definition.

self_check.prompt_text: What two functions make a business a bank under the definition?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Accepting deposits from the public and lending or investing them.

payload.title: Deposits by cheque, licensing and the use of the word bank
payload.core_explanation_md:
- **Deposits withdrawable by cheque (Section 49A):** only a **banking company**, the **Reserve Bank**, the **State Bank of India** or another body **notified by the Central Government** may accept them.
- **Non-banking financial companies** may accept public deposits but under **Reserve Bank directions** (Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act), not as banks.
- **Licence (Section 22):** a **licence from the Reserve Bank** is needed to **start or carry on banking**.
- **Name (Section 7):** a banking company **must use the word bank** in its name; **no other company, firm or individual** may use **bank, banker or banking**. **Exemptions** include subsidiaries of banks, associations of banks, **primary credit societies**, certain **co-operative societies** and the **State Bank and nationalised banks**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The licence and the name rules protect the public from unlicensed deposit-takers posing as banks.

self_check.prompt_text: Who needs a licence under Section 22 to carry on banking?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A banking company, which needs a licence from the Reserve Bank.

payload.title: Permitted and prohibited business of banks
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Permitted (Section 6(1), examples):** dealing in **bills of exchange**; **lending and advancing money**; **guarantee and indemnity business**; **realising property** that comes into the bank's possession in satisfaction of its claims; and other business the **Central Government notifies**.

**Prohibited (Section 8):** a bank shall **not engage in trading** or **undertake trading risks**; **buying, selling or bartering goods** is prohibited. *Goods* = every kind of **moveable property** except **actionable claims, stocks, shares, money, bullion and specie** and the instruments in Section 6(1). A bank **can realise securities** taken for a loan, can **buy, sell or barter for others** in connection with **bills for collection or negotiation** and can act as **executor or trustee**.

**Non-banking assets (Section 9):** a bank **cannot hold immovable property** acquired in satisfaction of claims for **more than seven years** (except for its own use); the Reserve Bank may extend by **up to five years** if in the **depositors' interest**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The rule keeps banks from taking trading risks with depositors money.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long may a bank hold immovable property acquired in satisfaction of claims?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not more than seven years, extendable by up to five years by the Reserve Bank.

payload.title: Constitution of banks in India
payload.core_explanation_md:
A bank in India is one of: a **body corporate under a special statute**; a **company** under the **Companies Act** (or a **foreign company**); or a **co-operative society** under a **Central or State enactment**.

| Type | Constituted under |
| --- | --- |
| **Public sector banks (other than SBI)** | **Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970 and 1980**: Section 3 vests the **undertakings of nationalised banks** in new statutory bodies |
| **State Bank of India** | **State Bank of India Act, 1955**; the seven associate banks (Subsidiary Banks Act, 1959) **merged with SBI**, completed in **2017-18** |
| **Regional Rural Banks** | **Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976** plus some provisions of the BR Act and RBI Act |
| **Private sector banks** (including micro and small finance banks) | **Companies Act** |
| **Foreign banks** | **Foreign companies**; certain Companies Act provisions apply; the **BR Act and RBI Act govern their banking business in India** |
| **Co-operative banks** | **Co-operative Societies Acts** (state or multi-state) |
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The founding statute decides which parts of the banking laws apply.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which Act were Regional Rural Banks constituted?

payload.title: Co-operative banks and dual control
payload.core_explanation_md:
A co-operative bank does ordinary banking on a **co-operative basis**. Structure: **urban co-operative banks** (scheduled or non-scheduled, multi-state or single-state) and **rural co-operatives**: **long term** (state and primary co-operative agriculture and rural development banks) and **short term** (**state co-operative banks**, **district central co-operative banks**, **primary agricultural credit societies**).

- **More than one state:** the **Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act**; otherwise the **State Co-operative Societies Act**.
- **Banking Laws (Application to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1965** extended parts of the BR Act and RBI Act to them (**Section 56** of the BR Act).
- **Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020** (after the **PMC Bank** failure) gave the Reserve Bank **more control** over **management, capital, audit and liquidation**, including **supersession of boards** and **restructuring**.
- Under Section 56 **references are modified**: banking company becomes **co-operative bank**; memorandum or articles become **bye-laws**; **Registrar of Companies** becomes the **Registrar of Co-operative Societies**.

**Dual control:** **State Governments and Registrars** control **formation, management and winding up**; the **Reserve Bank** controls **banking licence and regulation of banking business**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Two authorities share control, which is why co-operative bank failures needed a legal change.

self_check.prompt_text: Who controls the banking regulation of a co-operative bank and who controls its management as a society?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Reserve Bank regulates the banking business; the State Government and Registrar control its formation, management and winding up as a society.

payload.title: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose:** to constitute the Reserve Bank, to **regulate the issue of bank notes**, to **keep reserves** to secure **monetary stability** and to operate the **currency and credit system** to the country's advantage.

**What the Act deals with:** the **constitution, powers and functions** of the Reserve Bank; it does **not directly regulate banks**, except **Section 42** (**cash reserves** of scheduled banks with the Reserve Bank) and **Section 18** (**direct discount of bills**).

**Central Board:** a **Governor** and not more than **four Deputy Governors**; **four directors** (one from each **local board**); **ten directors** nominated by the Government; **two government officials**.

**Scheduled bank:** a bank in the **Second Schedule** of the Act, meeting the criteria of **Section 42(6)(a)**.

**Selected sections (as cited):** **3** constitution; **4** capital; **7** management; **8** Central Board; **17** business it may transact; **19** business it may not transact; **22** issue of notes; **30** supersession of the Central Board; **42** cash reserves.

**Lender of last resort:** the Reserve Bank offers funds to institutions in difficulty (**Sections 17 and 18**). **2019 amendments** gave it powers over **non-banking financial companies**: replace or supersede boards, **remove or debar auditors**, frame **schemes of amalgamation or splitting** and direct **group company information**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: As lender of last resort the central bank can prevent one bank failure becoming a systemic crisis.

self_check.prompt_text: Which section of the RBI Act deals with the cash reserves of scheduled banks?

payload.title: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Background:** passed as the **Banking Companies Act, 1949**, in force from **16 March 1949**; renamed the **Banking Regulation Act** from **1 March 1966**; **extended to co-operative banks** in **1965** by adding **Section 56**.

**Covers:** the **definition of banking**, **licensing**, **capital and reserve requirements**, **operations and management**, **liquidity**, **inspection**, and the **takeover, amalgamation and liquidation** of banks.

**Powers of the Reserve Bank:** **licence banks**, regulate **shareholding and voting rights**, supervise the **board and managers**, regulate **operations**, set **audit instructions**, order **moratorium, mergers and liquidation**, issue **directives** and **impose penalties**.

**Amendments (as the courseware describes):** **2017**: **Sections 35AA and 35AB** let the Reserve Bank direct banks to start **insolvency resolution** (under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code); **2012**: the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund** takes over **deposits inoperative for ten years**; the Reserve Bank conducts an **annual financial inspection** (**Section 35**) and **risk-based supervision**.

**Objectives:** give **specific legislation** for banking; **prevent bank failures** through **minimum capital**; ensure **balanced growth**; give the Reserve Bank **specific powers**; **safeguard depositors**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The Act is the main statute for the day-to-day regulation of banking companies.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two objectives of the Banking Regulation Act.
self_check.expected_takeaway: For example preventing bank failures through minimum capital, and safeguarding the interest of depositors.

payload.title: The Reserve Bank and the Government as regulators
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Reserve Bank powers as regulator and supervisor:** **issue licences**; **appoint and remove managerial personnel or boards**; **regulate business**; **give directions**; **inspect and supervise**; **audit**; **collect and furnish credit information**; **moratorium, amalgamation and winding up**; **impose penalties**. The **Department of Non-Banking Supervision** regulates **non-banking financial companies**.

**The Government's role:**

- It is the **sole shareholder** of the Reserve Bank and **appoints** its Governor and Central Board members.
- **Section 7(1) RBI Act:** it can give **directions in the public interest** after consulting the Governor (rarely used; first in **October 2018**, as the courseware says).
- **Appeals** lie to the Government against removal of managerial personnel (**Sections 10B and 36AA**), **cancellation of a banking licence** (**Section 22**) and refusal of a certificate on **floating charges** (**Section 14A**).
- It may **suspend or exempt** operations (**Sections 4 and 53**), **notify other banking business** (**Section 6(1)**), make **rules** (**Sections 52 and 45Y**), approve **subsidiaries** (**Section 19**), appoint a **court liquidator** (**Section 38A**) and **acquire undertakings** (**Section 36AE**).
- It holds **50 per cent or more** of the shares of **SBI, nationalised banks and RRBs** and so controls their management.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The Reserve Bank is the primary regulator but the Government keeps a layer of appellate and rule-making power.

payload.title: Regulation of banks by other authorities
payload.core_explanation_md:
A bank is also subject to **other regulators** in its other activities:

| Area | Authority |
| --- | --- |
| **Company matters** | **Companies Act** |
| **Workmen, premises, contract labour** | **Labour authorities** |
| **Taxes** | **Income tax, GST and others** |
| **Dealing in shares and debentures; public issue of capital** | **SEBI** (Securities Contract (Regulation) Act, 1956; SEBI Act, 1992) |
| **Insurance business** | **IRDAI** |
| **Mutual fund and merchant banking** | **Reserve Bank and SEBI** rules |

Under **Section 6** of the Banking Regulation Act banks may do **certain non-banking business** but in that case are **subject to the other agency's control**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A bank can be regulated by several bodies at the same time, each for a different activity.

self_check.prompt_text: Which authority regulates a bank public issue of capital?
self_check.expected_takeaway: SEBI (the Securities and Exchange Board of India).

items.title: Sources of banking regulation and the definition of banking
items.core_explanation_md:
Banking in India is governed mainly by the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**. The Reserve Bank and the Government control banks **from opening to winding up**.

**The provisions do not apply uniformly**: they depend on whether the bank is a **statutory corporation**, a **banking company** or a **co-operative society**.

**Definition (Section 5(b), as the courseware cites it):** *accepting, for the purpose of **lending or investing**, **deposits of money from the public**, **repayable on demand or otherwise** and **withdrawable by cheque, draft, order or otherwise**.*

So a bank does **two essential things:** **accepts deposits from the public** and **lends or invests** them. Accepting from the public does **not** mean accepting from anyone: a bank can **refuse undesirable customers**, and account opening follows **KYC norms**, with **suspicious transactions reported** under anti-money laundering rules.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A deposit-taker that does not lend or invest the deposits is not a bank under the definition.

self_check.prompt_text: What two functions make a business a bank under the definition?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Accepting deposits from the public and lending or investing them.

items.title: Deposits by cheque, licensing and the use of the word bank
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Deposits withdrawable by cheque (Section 49A):** only a **banking company**, the **Reserve Bank**, the **State Bank of India** or another body **notified by the Central Government** may accept them.
- **Non-banking financial companies** may accept public deposits but under **Reserve Bank directions** (Chapter IIIB of the RBI Act), not as banks.
- **Licence (Section 22):** a **licence from the Reserve Bank** is needed to **start or carry on banking**.
- **Name (Section 7):** a banking company **must use the word bank** in its name; **no other company, firm or individual** may use **bank, banker or banking**. **Exemptions** include subsidiaries of banks, associations of banks, **primary credit societies**, certain **co-operative societies** and the **State Bank and nationalised banks**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The licence and the name rules protect the public from unlicensed deposit-takers posing as banks.

self_check.expected_takeaway: A banking company, which needs a licence from the Reserve Bank.

items.title: Permitted and prohibited business of banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Permitted (Section 6(1), examples):** dealing in **bills of exchange**; **lending and advancing money**; **guarantee and indemnity business**; **realising property** that comes into the bank's possession in satisfaction of its claims; and other business the **Central Government notifies**.

**Prohibited (Section 8):** a bank shall **not engage in trading** or **undertake trading risks**; **buying, selling or bartering goods** is prohibited. *Goods* = every kind of **moveable property** except **actionable claims, stocks, shares, money, bullion and specie** and the instruments in Section 6(1). A bank **can realise securities** taken for a loan, can **buy, sell or barter for others** in connection with **bills for collection or negotiation** and can act as **executor or trustee**.

**Non-banking assets (Section 9):** a bank **cannot hold immovable property** acquired in satisfaction of claims for **more than seven years** (except for its own use); the Reserve Bank may extend by **up to five years** if in the **depositors' interest**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The rule keeps banks from taking trading risks with depositors money.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Not more than seven years, extendable by up to five years by the Reserve Bank.

items.core_explanation_md:
A bank in India is one of: a **body corporate under a special statute**; a **company** under the **Companies Act** (or a **foreign company**); or a **co-operative society** under a **Central or State enactment**.

| Type | Constituted under |

| **Public sector banks (other than SBI)** | **Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970 and 1980**: Section 3 vests the **undertakings of nationalised banks** in new statutory bodies |

items.title: Co-operative banks and dual control
items.core_explanation_md:
A co-operative bank does ordinary banking on a **co-operative basis**. Structure: **urban co-operative banks** (scheduled or non-scheduled, multi-state or single-state) and **rural co-operatives**: **long term** (state and primary co-operative agriculture and rural development banks) and **short term** (**state co-operative banks**, **district central co-operative banks**, **primary agricultural credit societies**).

- **More than one state:** the **Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act**; otherwise the **State Co-operative Societies Act**.
- **Banking Laws (Application to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1965** extended parts of the BR Act and RBI Act to them (**Section 56** of the BR Act).
- **Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020** (after the **PMC Bank** failure) gave the Reserve Bank **more control** over **management, capital, audit and liquidation**, including **supersession of boards** and **restructuring**.
- Under Section 56 **references are modified**: banking company becomes **co-operative bank**; memorandum or articles become **bye-laws**; **Registrar of Companies** becomes the **Registrar of Co-operative Societies**.

**Dual control:** **State Governments and Registrars** control **formation, management and winding up**; the **Reserve Bank** controls **banking licence and regulation of banking business**.

items.title: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
items.core_explanation_md:
**Purpose:** to constitute the Reserve Bank, to **regulate the issue of bank notes**, to **keep reserves** to secure **monetary stability** and to operate the **currency and credit system** to the country's advantage.

**What the Act deals with:** the **constitution, powers and functions** of the Reserve Bank; it does **not directly regulate banks**, except **Section 42** (**cash reserves** of scheduled banks with the Reserve Bank) and **Section 18** (**direct discount of bills**).

**Central Board:** a **Governor** and not more than **four Deputy Governors**; **four directors** (one from each **local board**); **ten directors** nominated by the Government; **two government officials**.

**Scheduled bank:** a bank in the **Second Schedule** of the Act, meeting the criteria of **Section 42(6)(a)**.

**Selected sections (as cited):** **3** constitution; **4** capital; **7** management; **8** Central Board; **17** business it may transact; **19** business it may not transact; **22** issue of notes; **30** supersession of the Central Board; **42** cash reserves.

**Lender of last resort:** the Reserve Bank offers funds to institutions in difficulty (**Sections 17 and 18**). **2019 amendments** gave it powers over **non-banking financial companies**: replace or supersede boards, **remove or debar auditors**, frame **schemes of amalgamation or splitting** and direct **group company information**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: As lender of last resort the central bank can prevent one bank failure becoming a systemic crisis.

items.title: The Banking Regulation Act, 1949
items.core_explanation_md:
**Background:** passed as the **Banking Companies Act, 1949**, in force from **16 March 1949**; renamed the **Banking Regulation Act** from **1 March 1966**; **extended to co-operative banks** in **1965** by adding **Section 56**.

**Covers:** the **definition of banking**, **licensing**, **capital and reserve requirements**, **operations and management**, **liquidity**, **inspection**, and the **takeover, amalgamation and liquidation** of banks.

**Powers of the Reserve Bank:** **licence banks**, regulate **shareholding and voting rights**, supervise the **board and managers**, regulate **operations**, set **audit instructions**, order **moratorium, mergers and liquidation**, issue **directives** and **impose penalties**.

**Amendments (as the courseware describes):** **2017**: **Sections 35AA and 35AB** let the Reserve Bank direct banks to start **insolvency resolution** (under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code); **2012**: the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund** takes over **deposits inoperative for ten years**; the Reserve Bank conducts an **annual financial inspection** (**Section 35**) and **risk-based supervision**.

**Objectives:** give **specific legislation** for banking; **prevent bank failures** through **minimum capital**; ensure **balanced growth**; give the Reserve Bank **specific powers**; **safeguard depositors**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Act is the main statute for the day-to-day regulation of banking companies.

items.title: The Reserve Bank and the Government as regulators
items.core_explanation_md:
**Reserve Bank powers as regulator and supervisor:** **issue licences**; **appoint and remove managerial personnel or boards**; **regulate business**; **give directions**; **inspect and supervise**; **audit**; **collect and furnish credit information**; **moratorium, amalgamation and winding up**; **impose penalties**. The **Department of Non-Banking Supervision** regulates **non-banking financial companies**.

**The Government's role:**

- It is the **sole shareholder** of the Reserve Bank and **appoints** its Governor and Central Board members.
- **Section 7(1) RBI Act:** it can give **directions in the public interest** after consulting the Governor (rarely used; first in **October 2018**, as the courseware says).
- **Appeals** lie to the Government against removal of managerial personnel (**Sections 10B and 36AA**), **cancellation of a banking licence** (**Section 22**) and refusal of a certificate on **floating charges** (**Section 14A**).
- It may **suspend or exempt** operations (**Sections 4 and 53**), **notify other banking business** (**Section 6(1)**), make **rules** (**Sections 52 and 45Y**), approve **subsidiaries** (**Section 19**), appoint a **court liquidator** (**Section 38A**) and **acquire undertakings** (**Section 36AE**).
- It holds **50 per cent or more** of the shares of **SBI, nationalised banks and RRBs** and so controls their management.
